snippet.title: Jaseiken Necromancer [邪聖剣ネクロマンサー] Game Sample -- PC Engine
snippet.description:
Jaseiken Necromancer (Also known as "Necromancer" and "The Necromancer", its title literally meaning "Wicked Holy Sword Necromancer") is the first traditional RPG released for the PC Engine, released during January of 1988. The game, like many console JRPGs of the 80s and early 90s, was modeled and largely influenced by the popularity and success of ChunSoft and Enix's "Dragon Quest" games, but also took some cues from Sega's "Phantasy Star" and distanced itself with a few "dynamic" aspects and a mature, mildly macabre world clearly inspired by the likes of H. P. Lovecraft and H.R. Giger... in fact, the game was inspired by H.R. Giger so much that his name is listed in the game's ending credits. A remake of the game is currently planned for Japanese Mobile phones and a DS adaptation known as "Jaseiken Necromancer: Nightmare Reborn" was released in 2010.

If the first Dragon Quest was about finding Erdrick's Sword, rescuing a princess, and slaying the Dragonlord, then this game essentially has the same premise, except they removed the princess and made the game more twisted as you find a demonic sword of immense power which can be good or evil depending on the wielder in an attempt to use it to defeat the vile "Great King Azatos" who will destroy the world if left unchecked. You play as a nameless hero who has traveled to the premiere "Kingdom of Randamelia" who is tasked with questing for the Necromancer Sword, and you are allowed to take two companions with you on your quest out of a possible five that the king has summoned. Outside of this, the vast majority of the dialogue is filler and cryptic messages ala "Dragon Quest" which will leave you scratching your head as you decipher riddles and wander the world in search of treasures and the whereabouts of the Necromancer.

The game is just like the early Dragon Quest games from opening menus to speaking and searching things to using a variety of keys to open various doors to even how one navigates caves and dungeons which have a restricted view and require magic or items to help illuminate the way. However, there are some subtle differences to the game's design that make it a more than competent contender of the era. For one, just having the ability to choose a party from the onset is a nice touch, and each character has strengths, weaknesses, and their tiny shred of personality. For instance, "Lime" is a sorceress who specializes more on HP and Attack than MP and Defense while other characters fill the role for a strongman, swift character, or "useless joke" character. The "useless joke" character is named "Romina" and she even admits that she's not very useful but loves you and possesses "the most attractive sprite in the game", pleading to join you. She has horrible stats, can't wear good equipment and is meant to make the game more challenging, but near the end of the game, her stats really improve and she has some interesting strengths. Besides growth differences, characters have different growth rates; mages are powerful but are the slowest levelers while the swift character (Maisuto), hero, and Romina are the fastest levelers.

Other things that helped the game stand-out is the ability to know ahead of time when characters are wounded and what they can/can't wear in shops, the ability to carry up to four of the same item, enemies with item drops, spells that can be purchased from shops, critical hits and "group barrages" (where a character can attack an enemy group multiple times consecutively), items to exit dungeons and return to the previous town you've visited, the ability to know how much exp. characters need by visiting just about any town's inn, and the ability to change rank and defend in battle. Another neat thing that needs to be brought up is that characters actually get stronger as a whole; while this sounds self-explanatory, a number of old games had a habit of only improving characters physically while their special abilities had preset damage or atrophy over time against more advanced adversaries. Not only do spells grow stronger as your characters do, but enemies have different strengths and immunities too. You could even power-level characters with a little trick by making two of the three characters escape from battle, increasing the experience a single character can get. The only things that bring the gameplay down is the absurdly high encounter rate (common to many Japanese RPGs of the era) and the ridiculously long passwords needed to continue (if you got a bad password, you were screwed).

The audio/visuals are only marginally better than NES/FC games of the time and comparable to SMS games like the original Phantasy Star (but on a less grand scale), using more realistically modeled characters, small-sized enemies with basic frames of animation, and simple music compositions, but this was still a great first RPG effort for owners of the PC Engine back in the day. The game is of pretty good length for an RPG of the time too.
